format_note: Rows are arrays matching `fields`, which keeps a large vocabulary readable and diffable. Empty strings and nulls are filled in by the loader; pronunciation and romanisation are computed by the phonology engine rather than stored, so they can never drift out of sync with the rules the app teaches. Add `detail` entries below for words needing synonyms, antonyms, collocations or counters.
words: The humble form. Use this with anyone you are not close to.
Only with close friends and people younger than you.
There are four people in my family.
Korean says 우리 where English says 'my' — 우리 엄마, 우리 나라.
Careful — sounds cold or confrontational. Koreans use names or titles instead.
님 is an honorific suffix. Also used to address any professional.
Native Korean. Becomes 한 before a counter: 한 개.
Sino-Korean. Used for dates, money, minutes, phone numbers.
Also sounds like 死 (death), so some buildings skip floor 4.
Korean counts in units of 10,000, not 1,000. 100,000 is 십만, not 백천.
How many are in your family?
My father is an office worker.
Korean sibling words depend on the speaker's gender.
Also used by women for slightly older male friends or partners.
My sister is a university student.
Gender-neutral. Add 남/여 to specify: 남동생, 여동생.
주무시다 is the honorific of 자다.
Also means 'a meal' generally. 밥 먹었어요? is a standard greeting.
I eat bread in the morning.
I eat a lot of fruit.
Carries flirtatious overtones in some contexts — a well-known film reference.
Same spelling as 차 'car'. Context decides.
Becomes a verb with 하다: 공부하다.
One of the first sentences worth memorising whole.
Shall we meet in the evening?
What are you doing this weekend?
I go to church on Sunday.
Same spelling as 눈 'eye'. Length differs in careful speech.
Three unrelated words with the same spelling.
Korean homes: shoes always come off at the door.
I have a lot of work.
I bought it at the market.
I have to go to the hospital.
to write; to use; to wear (hat)
여-irregular. Attaches to hundreds of nouns: 공부하다, 사랑하다.
to not exist, to not have
Takes 을/를. Contrast with 좋다, which takes 이/가.
Humble form when giving upward: 드리다.
ㄹ-stem: 압니다, 아세요. Negative is 모르다, not 안 알다.
I get off at the next station.
Regular ㅂ verb. Different verbs for hats (쓰다), shoes (신다), glasses (쓰다).
ㅂ-irregular: 더워요. For hot objects use 뜨겁다.
ㅂ-irregular: 추워요. For cold objects use 차갑다.
Regular — despite looking similar to 빠르다.
Works morning, noon and night. Literally 'are you at peace?'
Native Korean; 감사합니다 is Sino-Korean. Interchangeable in practice.
Say this if you are staying and they are going.
Say this if you are the one leaving.
Also used as 'uh-huh' to show you are listening.
Excuse me, may I ask directions?
Slightly stiff. Koreans often say 아니에요 instead.
Said before eating, especially if someone else is paying.
I was nervous about the exam.
Songs are 부르다 (called), not 노래하다 in careful speech.
Shortens to 좀, which also softens requests.
Strictly means 'excessively', but used for 'very' constantly.
One of the most useful sentences for a learner.

ko-v-0302.note_extra: 약을 먹다 (take medicine) and 나이를 먹다 (get older) both use 먹다 — Korean 'eats' more things than English does.

ko-v-0318.note_extra: 좋아하다 takes 을/를 because it is a verb. 좋다 takes 이/가 because it is an adjective. 김치를 좋아해요 but 김치가 좋아요 — both correct, different structures.

ko-v-0322.note_extra: There is no 안 알아요. The negative of 알다 is the separate verb 모르다.

ko-v-0339.note_extra: 걷다 meaning 'roll up' or 'collect' is regular (걷어요). Same spelling, different verb.

ko-v-0020.note_extra: Native numbers count things; Sino numbers read numbers. 두 시 삼십 분 uses both in one phrase.

ko-v-0091.note_extra: 차 'tea' and 차 'car' are different words with identical spelling and pronunciation.

ko-v-0223.note_extra: 배 means stomach, pear AND boat. Korean tolerates a lot of homonymy; context always disambiguates.
